body.text: Do political speeches matter anymore? Politicians love to give them, and journalists to report them. To be deemed worthy of proper attention a political announcement must come with a suitably intellectual analysis of the social or economic problem it is designed to tackle, dressed in high-flown rhetoric about political ideas and purpose, and win enthusiastic applause from those in the room.

Never mind that fewer than — let’s be generous — 0.01 per cent of the public have ever or would ever listen to a whole political speech; that most people’s attention span for the news now lasts no more than 280 characters or the length of a TikTok video; and that we have long since left behind the age of the commanding political orator — a Churchill, Roosevelt or Bob Hawke. A speech is still the chosen method of communication when a politician wants to be taken seriously.

So all eyes were on Andy Burnham when he gave his first big turn as British prime minister at the Labour Party’s annual conference in Liverpool on Tuesday. And he didn’t disappoint. Dressed in a suit but no tie, standing on the stage without a lectern (reading from autocues artfully positioned above and below eye level, so he could look up for idealism and down for seriousness), Burnham spoke for more than an hour. It was an electrifying performance.

He began with some personal history: the conference centre where he was speaking was just three miles from where his grandparents had bought their first house after the second world war, aspiring to a better standard of living in the new society that the postwar Labour government was building. He recalled how, growing up not much further away, his parents had imbued him and his brothers with the moral values of Christianity and the Labour Party, and encouraged him to go to Cambridge to get the education they had been denied. (He choked up and was briefly unable to continue when recalling his father, who died of dementia last month without knowing that his son had become prime minister.) How, after fifteen years as a member of parliament, he had become disillusioned with national politics and given up the job, but had then learned a new way of doing it — collaborative, practical, listening to people — in his nine years as mayor of Greater Manchester. And how he had decided to come back to Westminster now to change a failing system, both economic and political.
He acknowledged that professional politicians, including himself, had let the public down, and he apologised. But now, he declared, a line would be drawn under that failure.

Burnham’s analysis of Britain’s problems is nothing if not far-reaching. The country had been on a fundamentally wrong path since the 1980s, he said, since Margaret Thatcher launched her ideological revolution of privatisation, deregulation, deindustrialisation and political centralisation, later extended by austerity and Brexit. By putting the essentials of life — housing, transport, energy, water and social care — in the profit-seeking hands of the private sector, governments had been left with too little control to provide decent public services and hold down the cost of living.

Burnham makes no concession to the New Labour governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown in this analysis: in his view they did not fundamentally break with Thatcher’s project. (He has previously said he wants to end “forty years of neoliberalism.”) His mission as prime minister, he explained, was to put the country on a new path, reversing those trends to take back control of the economy and build a more caring society.

This was all rapturously received by the Labour members in the hall, who have been waiting at least thirty years to hear an electable Labour leader say such things. (The far-left leader Jeremy Corbyn said them between 2015 and 2020, but no one ever thought he would win an election.) They gave him multiple standing ovations, and tears were visible in some eyes.

Interestingly, Burnham’s most radical policy commitments were not for implementation now but ambitions for Labour’s next election manifesto in 2029. He wants to create a new National Care Service free at the point of use, complementing the National Health Service. This would partially be paid for by slowing the rise in the value of the state pension. He said he would establish a national commission to look at electoral reform, and introduce a fair voting system in the next parliament. And he held out the prospect of a new relationship with the European Union, including the possibility of rejoining.

It is unusual, to say the least, for a party leader to set out the main items of his next manifesto three years in advance, especially when they will involve inevitable tax increases, a change to the constitution and overturning a referendum result. But Burnham’s problem is not so much that his opponents will have a lot of time to take aim at these plans; he will equally have time to win support for them. It is that he will only win that election if he has done enough over the next three years for the public to allow him to continue.

Battered by an inexorably rising cost of living, stagnant real wages, unaffordable housing, failing public services and crumbling high streets, the British public is not in a forgiving mood. Not a single one of the last five British PMs (Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer) has managed to survive the political anger and alienation of the British electorate for any longer than three years.

Burnham was surprisingly vague about what he wants to do sooner rather than later. His anti-privatisation rhetoric has led many to assume he would renationalise the energy and water industries. But it seems not. A new division of the publicly owned Great British Energy company (established under Keir Starmer) will speed up electricity grid connections; but the privatised sector will otherwise remain as is. Thatcher’s prohibition on the state owning water companies would be repealed — but there were no plans for the legal power to be used. Devolution to newly empowered local authorities would restore economic growth “to every postcode” — but exactly how it was not clear. There will be a new focus on getting the young unemployed into vocational education, training or apprenticeships, thereby eventually cutting the UK’s spiralling welfare bill — but how this would be paid for in the short term, Burnham didn’t say.

He couldn’t say, because Britain’s public finances are in a parlous state and the bond markets are ready to pounce on any hint of higher spending or borrowing. The elevated oil price resulting from the war in Iran has led to a sell-off of government bonds across the world, but the interest rate on the UK’s (5.38 per cent for ten-year bonds this week, the highest for more than a quarter of a century) is above those in the rest of Europe, a product of its particular exposure to global energy prices and recent political instability. More than 8 per cent of the government budget now goes on debt interest payments, a fifty-year high, and recent borrowing has come in above forecasts.

Meanwhile, the share of taxes in national income is already at its highest level (38 per cent) since the 1980s, and the government will almost certainly have to raise taxes again in its budget later this month — not for higher spending on public services but just to balance the books with a sufficient buffer against unforeseen events. The Iran war continues to push up inflation (now over 3 per cent) and the Bank of England is likely to raise interest rates soon.

So Andy Burnham is squeezed between his ambitious rhetoric and straitened resources. The risk he faces is that this leads rapidly to public disillusionment, with voters seeing little change in their own or the nation’s circumstances and feeling let down again. In the opinion polls Labour has had a positive “Burnham bounce,” leapfrogging the far-right Reform UK (led by arch Brexiteer Nigel Farage) for the first time since March last year. But it is not a trampoline-sized bounce: Labour is less than four points ahead, and that margin hasn’t come from winning back Reform voters: it is some of those recently lost to the Greens and Liberal Democrats who have returned to the Labour fold.

Burnham’s speechmaking ability is not in doubt. But his ability to deliver on the ambitious promises he has made is at the mercy of global economic events he does not control, and he doesn’t have long to prove that the change Labour has promised will this time be real. As he stood basking in the applause this week the party’s new slogan shone brightly behind him: “Hope again.” Andy Burnham will be doing a lot of the hoping himself. •
